opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was one of the most important things that happened to me early on. Before that, I had this very abstract, almost mythologised picture of what a "researcher" was: someone who was just obviously brilliant in some way I wasn't, who always knew what the right question was, and who had this clear, confident path from idea to result. And so the idea that *I* could do that work felt a bit absurd.

Actually sitting down and talking with people who were doing the work punctured that in a really healthy way. You realise they're just people. They're confused a lot of the time. They have half-formed ideas, they try things that don't work, they change their minds. They'd say things like, "Oh yeah, I spent three weeks on that and it was a dead end." And that was weirdly reassuring, because I'd been interpreting my own confusion as evidence that I wasn't cut out for it, when actually confusion is just what research feels like from the inside.

The other thing was that it made the work concrete. Instead of "AI safety research" being this big nebulous thing, I could see what someone actually did day to day: writing code, running experiments, staring at plots, arguing about what a result means. And I could ask myself, "Do I enjoy that? Am I any good at that?" in a much more grounded way. A lot of it turned out to be stuff I genuinely found fun.

And I think the meta-lesson I'd pass on to listeners is that people are often much more willing to talk than you'd expect. Sending a short, thoughtful message to someone whose work you've actually engaged with has a surprisingly high hit rate, and even one or two conversations can dramatically shift your sense of whether something is a realistic path for you. It's very cheap information, and most people dramatically under-use it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says talking with researchers showed him they were ordinary, often-confused people, which reassured him that he could do the work too.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was pretty transformative. I think there's this mental model a lot of people have where researchers are these mythical beings who live in a different world, and research is this thing that other people do. And when you're an undergrad, or even a grad student, it's very easy to feel like there's an enormous gulf between where you are and where they are.

What I found when I actually started talking to people — and this was mostly through things like going to EA Global, reaching out to people whose work I'd read, doing internships — was that they're just people. They have the same confusions, they're uncertain about a lot of things, they got into the field through fairly contingent paths. And crucially, a lot of them were actively excited to talk to someone who was interested and had thought a bit about their work.

I think the biggest shift was going from "I'd need to be some kind of genius to do this" to "Oh, this is a job that people do, and the way you become one of them is you start doing the thing." Like, interpretability in particular was a really young field when I got into it. There just weren't that many people, and the ones who existed were very happy to have more. Chris Olah's team at Anthropic took me on, and I learned an enormous amount from just being around people doing it and seeing that the day-to-day is a lot of staring at confusing plots and being wrong, rather than having brilliant insights in the shower.

The other thing I'd flag is that talking to people gave me a much more accurate sense of what the field actually needed, versus what I imagined it needed from the outside. From the outside you see the polished papers. From the inside you see all the low-hanging fruit nobody's gotten to, the tooling that doesn't exist, the obvious follow-up experiments nobody's run. And that's incredibly motivating, because it means there's a concrete thing you can go do tomorrow that would actually be useful.

So I'd really encourage people to just reach out. Be specific, show you've engaged with their work, don't take it personally if they don't reply. But the expected value is very high, and I think most people underrate how approachable researchers are.

r001.rationale: He says researchers seemed mythical and far removed, but talking to them showed they were ordinary, approachable people. That shifted his view toward research being a job he could pursue by starting to do the work.

astra-6.text:
I think it made it feel much more like something I could actually do. There’s a big difference between reading someone’s work and thinking, “Wow, this person is incredibly smart,” and having a conversation where you can ask questions, follow their reasoning, and maybe contribute an idea of your own.

It also helped demystify research. From the outside, you see the polished result, and it’s easy to imagine that the person knew what they were doing the whole time. Talking to researchers gives you more of a sense that they’re figuring things out as they go, too. You don’t need to already know how to solve the problem to start working on it.

So I think those conversations shifted research from this abstract, impressive thing that other people did to a career I could seriously consider trying.

r001.rationale: The response says talking with researchers showed that they were figuring things out as they went, which made research feel like a career Neel could seriously consider pursuing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it made the whole thing feel much more real. Before that, I had this picture of researchers as these incredibly impressive people who were somehow fundamentally different from me. And then you talk to them, and they’re people. They’re confused about things, they have intuitions, they try stuff, and sometimes it doesn’t work. That made it much easier to imagine myself doing research.

And there’s a big difference between reading a paper, where everything has been polished into a coherent story, and talking to someone about how they actually figured it out. Seeing a bit of that messy process helped me think, “Oh, maybe this is something I could learn to do.”

r001.rationale: He says established researchers seemed like people rather than fundamentally different from him, which made it much easier to imagine himself doing research.
